sentences.text: The petitioner is the first accused in S.T. No. 63 of 2012 on the files of the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kozhikode.

The offences alleged are punishable under Sections 2(ia) (m) and 7(i) read with Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short 'the P.F.A. Act')
and Rule 5 Appendix B.A. 16.27 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, (for short "the PFA Rules").
2.
Heard.
3. The petitioner has filed this Crl. M.C. praying for quashing the complaint and further proceedings against the petitioner in the above case.

4. The prosecution allegation is that on 4-7-2207 at 10 a.m., the Food Inspector purchased 750 gms of tomato ketchup from the hotel, wherein the petitioner was the Manager and the second accused was the nominee.
After complying with the legal formalities, one sample was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.
The Public Analyst issued certificate of analysis, which would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for tomato ketchup and therefore, it was adulterated.
Thereafter, on the request of the petitioner, the 2 nd sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.
Annexure- A5 is the report of analysis.
Annexure-A5 would show that the sample analysed in the Laboratory did not conform to the standards for tomato sauce or ketchup as per the PFA Rules.

5. The learned counsel for the petitioner has argued that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act, Annexure-A5 report of the Central Food Laboratory,
cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.

The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.
6.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was held by the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report.
7. The Division Bench of this Court in Rasheed v. Food Inspector [2016 (2) KLT 390] considered the above question on a reference by a learned Single Judge.

The Division Bench in Rasheed (supra)
held that if an analysis is required to initiate prosecution, there should be notified laboratory and Rajeev vs Food Insector on 23 January, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150012299/
2 validated method of analysis as mandated under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act for a successful prosecution as held by the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

sentences.text:
8. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)
(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Annexure-A5 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).
Therefore, no successful prosecution can be maintained against the petitioner.
Consequently, no purpose will be served even if the prosecution against the eptitioner is permitted to be continued.

In the said circumstances, I am inclined to quash the final report and further proceedings against the petitioner in S.T. 63 of 2012 on the files of the court below, in exercise of the inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C., to meet the ends of justice.
It is ordered accordingly.
In the result, this Crl.M.C. stands allowed .
Dated this the 23rd day of January, 2019.
